H1.text: A bow pulled back. A wound-up toy car. A rock at a cliff edge.

H2.text: None of them is moving. Yet each one is ready to make something move.

H3.text: Diya holds a stretched catapult, perfectly still. On the roof, a full water tank sits perfectly still.

H4.text: Let go, and the stone flies. Open a tap, and water gushes. Where was that energy?

H5.text: It was stored. Today we meet the energy that waits: potential energy.

P2.text: It is energy stored because of where a body is, or the shape it is in.

P3.text: The tank stores it by its position, high up. The catapult stores it by its shape, stretched.

P4.text: Potential means possible. The energy is not moving yet, but it can come out as motion.

P5.text: Its symbol is U, and like all energy, it is measured in joules.

S1.text: Let's run Diya's catapult. The band behaves like a spring of two hundred newtons per metre.

S2.text: She pulls the pouch back slowly, twenty centimetres. The band pulls harder and harder, up to forty newtons.

S3.text: Her hand does work against the band. That work is stored as U: four joules.

S4.text: She lets go. The band pulls the eighty gram stone forward, and the stone flies off.

S5.text: Slow-mo replay, a hundred times slower.

S6.text: Now the band's force and the motion point the same way. The band does positive work.

S7.text: As the band shortens, U drains away, and the stone's kinetic energy grows.

S8.text: At the end, U is zero, and K is four joules. The stone leaves at ten metres per second.

C1.text: So a force can fill U, or empty it. Side by side.

C2.text: Lifting a ball. Gravity pulls down, the ball moves up. Gravity does negative work, and U goes up.

C3.text: Dropping the ball. Gravity pulls down, the ball moves down. Gravity does positive work, and U goes down.

C4.text: Now you try. A falling ball. Gravity does plus five joules of work on it. Does U go up or down, and by how much? Pause and decide.

C5.text: Down, by five joules! The force's work comes out of the store. W equals minus delta U.

D1.text: Now the rule, one step at a time.

D2.text: Step one. To fill the store slowly, your push balances the force. Your force is minus F.

D3.text: Step two. Your work is stored. So delta U equals minus the integral of F d x.

D4.text: Step three. For one tiny step, d U equals minus F d x.

D5.text: Step four. Divide by d x. F equals minus d U by d x.

D6.text: Check with gravity, up positive. U equals m g h, so d U by d h is m g, and F is minus m g. Downwards. It works.

T1.text: Remember this. The force is minus the slope of U. It always pushes toward lower U.

R1.text: Why the minus sign? Follow the links.

R2.text: One. Where U rises as x increases, the slope is positive.

R3.text: Two. The minus sign makes F negative there. The force points back, toward lower U.

R4.text: Three. Where U falls as x increases, F is positive. Again toward lower U.

R5.text: Four. Where the slope is flat, the force is zero. Like a ball resting at the bottom of a bowl.

K1.text: Your turn. On a U against x graph, U drops steeply as x increases. Which way does the force point? Pause and think.

K2.text: Along plus x! Toward lower U. And steeper means a bigger force.

W2.text: A particle has U equals three x squared minus twelve x joules. Find the force at one metre, and where the force is zero.

W3.text: F is minus d U by d x. d U by d x is six x minus twelve.

W4.text: So F equals twelve minus six x.

W5.text: At one metre, F is twelve minus six, six newtons, along plus x.

W6.text: F is zero when six x equals twelve. At two metres, the bottom of the U curve.

X2.text: Many students drop the minus sign. They write F equals d U by d x, and get minus six newtons.

X3.text: But the force points toward lower U. Keep the minus sign: F equals minus d U by d x.

E1.text: Where is this asked? In questions that give U as a formula or a graph, and ask for the force or the work.

Q1.text: Exam level now. U equals x squared minus four x joules. A particle moves from x equals one to x equals four metres. Find the work done by the force, and the force at four metres. Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is A. Minus three joules, and minus four newtons.

A2.text: U at one metre is minus three, at four metres zero. So delta U is plus three.

A3.text: Work by the force is minus delta U. Minus three joules.

A4.text: F is minus d U by d x, minus two x plus four. At four metres, minus four newtons.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these without help?

Y2.text: One. Where is the energy in a stretched catapult that is not moving?

Y3.text: Two. Gravity does ten joules of work on a falling ball. What happens to its U?

Y4.text: Three. Why does F equals minus d U by d x carry a minus sign?

N1.text: Next time: water from a rooftop tank gushes out of a tap. How much energy does height give it? Gravitational potential energy.
